‍


A user running one AI agent had no problems.


Running 10 at once exposed a problem that would change the direction of an entire startup.


The issue started with something simple.


A workflow automation tool let users take a CSV containing a list of people and run automated tasks on portions of that list.


When someone ran a workflow once, everything worked.


But some users wanted to run 10 workflows simultaneously.


That's when things broke.


Each agent would read the same saved position in the CSV before the others could update it.


Instead of processing different records, multiple agents ended up doing the same work.


For Thomas Karatzas, Co-Founder & CEO of Terse (YC F26), the problem revealed a much bigger opportunity.


Coordinating multiple AI agents that share state requires infrastructure that handles concurrency, persistence, and recovery.


Rather than continuing to build workflow automation tools, the team decided to build the underlying infrastructure.


That became the new direction for Terse.


Its solution is Durable Actors.


Each actor gets its own persistent state and SQLite database, with requests coordinated to prevent the race conditions that caused the original problem.


Consider an AI evaluation that takes 10 hours to complete.


If the process crashes halfway through, developers without durable execution may lose their progress or struggle to recover it.


With Terse, applications can persist state as work progresses, allowing interrupted tasks to recover without starting over.


The same infrastructure supports coordinating large numbers of AI agents, managing shared application state, and building real-time applications where humans and agents work together.


And Terse is making its actor runtime open source, giving developers the option to run the infrastructure themselves rather than relying exclusively on a hosted service.


What began as a problem with 10 agents processing a CSV helped reveal an infrastructure challenge that becomes increasingly important as AI applications scale.


Sometimes the most valuable part of a product is the infrastructure you had to build to make it work.
